markets.say: Alright, this is Module 1, Markets, and we start with where securities actually come from. Most people buy through an intermediary, like a bank, broker, dealer or mutual fund. The investment bank helps a company or municipality raise capital by underwriting new securities or acting as the issuer's agent, and in an IPO it usually prices the deal the day before shares go to the public. Why so late? Under a firm commitment the underwriter buys the whole issue at a set price and resells it, so pricing late limits its exposure to market moves. That's the contrast to burn in. Firm commitment, the underwriter eats the unsold shares. Best efforts, the issuer gets nothing for shares that don't sell. Walk Kestrel Labs: three million shares offered at twelve dollars, but investors only take two point six million. Firm commitment, Kestrel still gets proceeds on all three million, thirty-six million dollars before fees, and the underwriter is stuck with four hundred thousand shares. Best efforts, Kestrel gets only thirty-one point two million. Quick vocabulary: the red herring is the preliminary prospectus, filed but not yet effective, so no sales; the green shoe is the right to enlarge the offering; the lockup, often a hundred eighty days, keeps insiders from selling. The exam trap: a broker is an agent paid by commission, a dealer trades from its own inventory for the spread, and specialists and market makers are both dealers. To a client with pre-IPO shares: you agreed to a lockup, so let's plan your diversification for the day it lifts instead of counting on today's price.

Next, the private side of the market. Venture capital funds private, often start-up companies, usually through convertible preferred stock. It's high risk, high potential return, illiquid, and has low correlation with stocks. VC firms take a big equity stake, advise management, and hope to exit in about five to ten years, ideally through an IPO, counting on a few big winners to offset the outright losses. The stages run from seed money before a product exists, through mezzanine for expansion and bridge financing to an expected IPO. Private placements sell an issue, most often bonds, to a small group of institutions or sophisticated investors, skipping SEC registration and IPO selling costs. The limit is thirty-five non-accredited buyers and unlimited accredited ones. So who's accredited? An individual needs net worth over one million dollars, alone or with a spouse, excluding the primary residence, or income over two hundred thousand, three hundred thousand joint, in each of the last two years with the same expected this year. Walk Nadia: one point three million net worth, but four hundred fifty thousand is home equity, so she's at eight hundred fifty thousand and fails. Her income was two hundred ten thousand last year but one ninety the year before, so she fails that too. You can't average. In a limited partnership, the general partner runs it with unlimited liability; limited partners get no management role and limited liability. The exam trap: venture capital is illiquid, so any answer calling it highly liquid is wrong. To a client eyeing a partnership: you'd have no say in how it's run, you probably couldn't sell when you need cash, and the income isn't tax-free.

Now how trading actually works. The primary market is the first sale of new securities, and that cash, less underwriting costs, goes to the issuer. The secondary market is investors trading with each other, from the first market, exchange auction trading like the NYSE, to the fourth, institutions trading big blocks directly with no broker. On custody, street name means the broker holds your shares, and SIPC covers up to five hundred thousand dollars per customer, max two hundred fifty thousand in cash, but never market losses. The orders are where the exam lives. A market order fills now at the best available price, with no price control. A limit order sets a ceiling to buy or a floor to sell. A stop triggers at or through the stop and becomes a market order; a stop-limit becomes a limit order. Watch Ana: she sets a sell order at fifty. Bad news overnight, and the stock opens at forty-three. With a plain stop, the open is through fifty, so it fills near forty-three. With a stop-limit at fifty, nothing fills at forty-three, and if it keeps sliding she still owns it. Sell stops go below the market, buy stops above, so a short seller protects himself with a buy stop. The trap in one line: stop means execution is certain but price isn't; stop-limit means price is certain but execution isn't. To a client: a stop gets you out, maybe well below your number; a stop-limit protects the price but may leave you holding the stock. Which risk bothers you more?

markets.at: Short sales, margin and leveraged returns
markets.say: This is leverage, and it's formula-heavy, so let's go slow. A short seller borrows shares, sells them, then buys them back to cover, profiting if the price falls. They post a deposit, currently fifty percent of market value, and any dividend paid while short goes to the lender. Margin buying uses the same idea: initial margin is fifty percent under Regulation T, and maintenance, set by the broker, is usually thirty-five percent. Equity is market value minus what you owe. Short return first. Wes shorts a hundred shares at eighty, posting four thousand dollars, pays a fifty-cent dividend, and covers at seventy. Gross gain a thousand, minus fifty in dividends, nine fifty, over his four thousand deposit: twenty-three point seven five percent. Now the margin call. Lena buys at forty with fifty percent margin, so her loan is twenty dollars a share. The call price is the loan over one minus maintenance, twenty over point six five, about thirty seventy-seven. If the stock drops to twenty-six, required equity is twenty-six times thirty-five percent, nine ten, but actual equity is only six dollars, so she deposits three ten a share, three thousand one hundred on a thousand shares. And holding period return on margin divides by the investor's own money: Omar's twenty percent cash return becomes thirty-four percent leveraged, after interest, and a minus twelve percent loss becomes minus thirty. The traps: use the current price, not the purchase price, for the deposit, and divide by the investor's money, not the full position. To a client: borrowing to invest doubles the swing both ways, so let's size this so a margin call can't force your hand.

Cash and cash equivalents. In planning that means bank deposits and money market instruments with high liquidity, and the interest is ordinary income. First, a distinction the exam loves: liquidity versus marketability. Liquid means cash quickly at a known price with no real principal loss. Marketable means you can sell quickly in an identifiable market, but the price isn't assured. A money market deposit account is liquid but not marketable, because only the bank redeems it; a T-bill is both. Now the lineup. CDs run one month to five years, with an early-redemption penalty and FDIC coverage. The money market deposit account is a bank product, FDIC insured. The money market mutual fund is an investment company, not insured. T-bills sell at a discount with no default risk, and the interest is federally taxed but state and local exempt; the thirteen-week bill is the risk-free proxy in pricing models. Commercial paper is unsecured corporate notes, two hundred seventy days max. Walk June: she buys a ten-thousand-dollar thirteen-week T-bill for ninety-nine hundred. Income is one hundred dollars, and her return is one hundred over ninety-nine hundred, about one point oh one percent. Divide by what she paid, not face. At twenty-two percent federal and five percent state, she pays twenty-two dollars of tax versus twenty-seven on a CD, saving five dollars of state tax. The trap: the MMDA is insured, the money market fund isn't. To a client: cash is great for your emergency fund and near-term bills, but beyond that inflation quietly eats it, and losing buying power can be a bigger risk than losing principal.

Now taxes, starting with a map of who taxes what. Treasury interest: federal yes, state no. Corporate bond interest: both. Municipal interest: generally federally exempt, but state-taxed unless it's from your home state. Dividends and capital gains: both. Qualified dividends from C corporations get the zero, fifteen or twenty percent rates, but only if you meet the holding period: more than sixty days in the hundred-twenty-one-day window that starts sixty days before the ex-dividend date. REIT and S corporation dividends are not qualified, because there's no entity-level tax first. Then the net investment income tax: three point eight percent times the lesser of net investment income or MAGI over the threshold, which is two hundred fifty thousand married filing jointly, one twenty-five married filing separately, and two hundred thousand for others. The word lesser is the whole game. Two couples, each with sixty thousand of investment income. The Parks have MAGI of four hundred ten thousand, an excess of one sixty, so the lesser is sixty thousand and the tax is two thousand two hundred eighty dollars. The Cruzes have MAGI of two ninety, an excess of forty thousand, so the lesser is forty thousand and they owe fifteen hundred twenty. The trap: dividend does not always mean preferential rates. REIT and S corp payouts don't qualify, and neither does a C corp dividend if the holding period is missed. To a client: your Treasury interest skips state tax, in-state munis skip both, and REIT dividends are taxed like wages, so where each holding sits can change your tax bill without changing your risk.

markets.at: Capital gain netting and wash sales
markets.say: Last section of this tab: capital gains. Held more than a year is long term; a year or less is short term. Net long-term gains get the zero, fifteen, twenty percent rates, with two exceptions: collectibles max out at twenty-eight percent, and gain from real-estate depreciation at twenty-five. Netting goes in order: short-term against short-term, long-term against long-term, then cross-net if one side is a gain and the other a loss. A net loss deducts up to three thousand dollars a year, with the rest carried forward indefinitely. Walk Grant: long-term gain fourteen thousand, loss five, so plus nine thousand. Short-term gain three thousand, loss eighteen, so minus fifteen. Cross-net, and he has a six-thousand-dollar net short-term loss. He deducts three thousand now and carries three thousand forward. Nothing is forfeited. Then wash sales: sell at a loss and acquire similar securities within thirty days before or after, and the loss is postponed, not lost. It's added to the replacement shares' basis. Sofia bought for ninety-six hundred and sold for seventy-eight hundred, an eighteen-hundred-dollar loss, then bought back ten days later for seventy-five hundred. Recognized loss is zero, and her new basis is seventy-five hundred plus eighteen hundred, ninety-three hundred dollars, or sixty-two a share. Add the loss, don't subtract it. The traps: the three-thousand limit applies after cross-netting, and the wash-sale window looks thirty days backward as well as forward. To a client: we can book this loss to offset gains, but if we buy the same stock back within a month the IRS just tacks it onto the new shares, so let's wait out the window or hold something similar but not the same.
